narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your class ranking in the third year of law school, and your family income level. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. It sits well below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation for the demands of the bar exam.

Your third-year class ranking worked in the opposite direction. At 6.00 it was slightly better than the 5.79 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the prediction modestly toward passing. Your middle family income also contributed a smaller push toward failure, though this factor carried far less weight than your grades.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic record created too high a risk of failing the bar exam, outweighing the few positive signals in your profile.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake challenging courses to raise your GPA, seek academic support early in law school to improve your class standing, and consider bar-prep programs with proven first-time pass rates. Once you can demonstrate stronger academic performance, reapply; many students improve their profiles and gain admission on a second attempt.
